source.title: f-INE: A Hypothesis Testing Framework for Estimating Influence under Training Randomness
source.authors: Subhodip Panda; Dhruv Tarsadiya; Shashwat Sourav; AP Prathosh; Sai Praneeth Karimireddy

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures data-influence estimates under training randomness and their utility for identifying mislabeled or poisoned data. It does not measure the listed versions' training-versus-test generalization claims or the properties named in those versions.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses training randomness and reports classification test accuracy and influence-estimation results, but those results do not test the claim versions. MNIST test accuracy and influence-ranking results are outside the specified training/test gap outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates influence estimation, mislabeled-data detection, and deliberately induced LLM sentiment steering. It cites original sources associated with V3 and V8 but does not test their claims. In particular, self-influence rankings are not followed by removal and retraining comparisons against random removal.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete: the authors frame influence through hypothesis testing over training randomness, derive composition and asymptotic Gaussian properties, and propose efficient estimation from one training run. They report lower influence-score variability and improved mislabeled- or poisoned-data identification against several baselines, with classification detection comparable to TraceIn.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates influence estimation and data attribution under training randomness, rather than the generalization interventions or measurements in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Influence-estimation outcomes vary with data-shuffling order, random seeds, gradient projection dimension, number of checkpoints, and the compared influence method.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-influence rankings identify deliberately mislabeled MNIST and CIFAR-10 examples; f-INE performs comparably to TraceIn and better than the other tested baselines.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Influence rankings can identify mislabeled training examples; this does not establish the accuracy consequences of removing highly memorized examples.

fits_no_version.finding: f-INE influence scores vary less across training runs than comparison methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Influence-estimation methods differ in robustness to training randomness.

fits_no_version.finding: Poisoned instruction tuning increases negative responses, and f-INE identifies the poisoned instructions more effectively than LESS.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Influence estimation can attribute deliberately induced sentiment steering to poisoned training instructions.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix E reports 97% MNIST test accuracy for an MLP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An MLP achieves high MNIST accuracy under the reported training setup; this isolated result supplies none of the comparisons required by V1–V8.

record.problems: Influence-estimation experiments use three random training runs for the reported LLM comparisons; several findings are presented as plots. These do not bear on the claim versions' generalization-gap outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: the reported results concern influence consistency, influence ranking, or poisoned-data identification, not a version's specified generalization outcome.

untested.parts: Near-perfect random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe, with chance held-out performance on random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer held-out performance under specified tuning budgets.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout interventions and their interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps and competing generalization measures.
Test accuracy after removing highly memorized examples and retraining, compared with equally many random removals.

record.verdict_notes: The empty result-row set is appropriate for these claim versions. Appendix E's architecture descriptions differ from those in the main classification experiments, but neither description supplies a qualifying architecture comparison. No version-specific verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Whether the same recipes fit random labels and generalize on natural labels.
Whether test error keeps falling beyond interpolation as width increases.
Comparative test error of convolutional and fully connected networks, and the role of local connectivity.
Held-out performance comparisons between adaptive and non-adaptive optimizers.
The effect of batch size and adapted training recipes on the generalization gap.
The effect of dropout and its interaction with training-set size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Whether magnitude-aware sharpness tracks the train/test gap.
Whether removing memorized examples reduces test accuracy relative to random removals.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
